# Succinate

**Succinate** (succinic acid, C4H6O4) is the four-carbon intermediate of the [[Citric Acid Cycle]] generated by [[Succinate Dehydrogenase]] (complex II) from [[α-Ketoglutarate]]-derived oxalosuccinate and converted to fumarate by the same enzyme. Beyond its role as an electron donor into the respiratory chain, it is a signalling metabolite that couples metabolic state to transcription and to inflammation.

## Mechanism & Metabolic Roles

- **TCA / respiratory coupling:** succinate is oxidised to fumarate by complex II, whose activity also sets the NADH/FADH2 supply for [[Oxidative Phosphorylation]].
- **Pseudo-hypoxia:** inhibition of SDH (e.g. by tumour metabolites, or in HIF pathway crosstalk) causes succinate accumulation, which inhibits the prolyl hydroxylases responsible for HIF-α degradation, stabilising HIF-1α and inducing a hypoxia-like transcriptional programme even at normal oxygen.
- **Succination (not succinylation):** succinate reacts with cysteine thiols to form S-(2-succino)cysteine, an irreversible covalent modification distinct from reversible succinylation; it impairs protein function and is a marker of oxidative/mitochondrial stress.
- **Reverse electron transport:** a high succinate/SDH ratio drives ROS production at complex I, linking the metabolite to [[Reactive Oxygen Species|ROS]] and to redox signalling.
- **Inflammation:** succinate accumulates in activated macrophages and stabilises HIF-1α, driving IL-1β maturation; this is the basis of the "succinate → HIF-1α → IL-1β" axis and of succinate's reputation as a pro-inflammatory metabolite (in contrast to itaconate, which is anti-inflammatory).
- **Other positions:** succinate is a substrate for porphyrin synthesis (haem) and for gluconeogenesis via oxaloacetate; the succinate/succinate-to-fumarate ratio is used as a proxy for mitochondrial redox state.

## Clinical Relevance

Succinate accumulation is described in ischaemia–reperfusion injury, in mitochondrial disease (SDH/SDHA/Fumarate Hydratase mutations in hereditary paraganglioma–pheochromocytoma and leiomyomatosis), in inflammatory bowel disease and in tumours (SDH-deficient GISTs, HIF-driven cancers). Urinary succinate and succinylated proteins are emerging readouts of mitochondrial and oxidative stress.
